the-sun.essay:
The Sun is a star, a ball of extremely hot gas at the centre of the solar system. It lies about 149.6 million kilometres from Earth and measures about 1.4 million kilometres across. It has no solid ground, and no one can go there. A territory on the Sun therefore cannot be a physical place. Every attempt to create one has been a matter of paper, and all of it has happened on Earth. The limits come from people and offices here, such as the notary who records a statement, the rules of the website used to sell plots, and a local court.

To see why a paper claim achieves so little, it helps to start with what ownership is. When a person owns a house, a government keeps a record of that ownership, its courts will settle a dispute over it, and its police will remove a trespasser. Ownership depends on a government standing behind it. Space has a special rule that removes that support. The Outer Space Treaty, which took effect in 1967, is the main treaty on what countries may do in space. Article II says that outer space, including the Moon and other natural bodies in space, is not subject to "national appropriation", meaning a country taking it as its own, whether by claiming authority over it, by using or occupying it, or by any other means. If no country may claim the Sun, no country has authority to hand out title to pieces of it.

The argument on the other side is about the treaty's wording. Article II mentions nations and says nothing directly about private people. María Ángeles Durán of Vigo in Spain argues that this stops countries from owning a star and leaves individuals free to do so. Dennis Hope, a Nevada entrepreneur who sells deeds to the Moon, reads the treaty the same way. Most space lawyers disagree, according to a review of the writing on the point in the law blog Völkerrechtsblog. They point to Article VI, which makes each country answer for the space activity of its private companies and citizens, and says such activity needs permission and continuing oversight from a treaty member. A private person is therefore still acting under a country's responsibility. Spain has joined the Outer Space Treaty. It has not joined the Moon Agreement, a separate treaty with 17 members, whose Article 11 says plainly that no natural person may own the surface of the Moon, and whose Article 1 extends its Moon rules to other natural bodies in the solar system apart from Earth. Neither treaty defines "celestial body", the term in the original text, though the Sun is ordinarily described as one. No court is confirmed to have ruled on any of this for the Sun, so the wording argument remains open in that narrow sense.

Durán's case shows what happens at each step. In 2010 she went to a notary, an official who certifies legal documents. The notary recorded her statement that she was "owner of the Sun, type G2 star". The Spanish news site Genbeta says the notary did not take it seriously, asked the notaries' professional body, and was told to record what she said. That is the limit of what such a document does. It proves a person made a statement on a certain day. It does not prove the statement is true, and it gives no sovereignty, meaning a government's full authority over a place. Genbeta adds that the Spanish property registry has no power over the solar system, so her claim could not be entered there.

She gave a second legal reason, usucapion, an old rule inherited from Roman law under which long use of a thing can turn into ownership of it. Her point was that she had benefited from sunlight for decades. Everyone else on Earth has done the same.

Next came the money. She threatened to charge people for using solar power, later saying she had meant electricity companies. No payment is known to have been made. She then sold plots on eBay, the online auction site, at 1 euro per square metre, with a certificate for each. About two years after she opened the account, eBay removed the listings under its policy on intangible goods, meaning things that cannot be physically delivered, and blocked her account. A private website needs no treaty to do this, because its own rules decide what may be sold on it.

She sued eBay in court number 5 of Alcobendas, near Madrid. The amount is reported as 10,000 euros by The Register and about 7,500 pounds by Scottish Financial News. Accounts of the result differ. A report from June 2015 said a Spanish court recognised her claim and let her pursue the dispute, with a first hearing set for 17 June 2015. The Mexican newspaper Excelsior said in 2022 that the court declared itself competent and let her sue, and it dated recognition of her ownership to 2012 without citing documents. Genbeta later wrote that the court dismissed the case and that a Spanish court said in 2016 that a person cannot legally own the Sun. It names no court document and credits Excelsior, whose article does not say this. How the case finally ended is not confirmed. A court that admits a case for hearing has agreed only to listen to it. Letting someone sue is a different thing from finding that she owns what she claims, and no confirmed ruling says she owns the Sun.

Suppose a claimant now sends an invoice to a solar power company. The company can simply refuse, and the claimant must then go to court and prove ownership with a document that only records her own words. Gregory Nemitz, an American, claimed the asteroid Eros and sent NASA a bill for $20 when its probe landed there. NASA refused, the State Department said Article II rules out private ownership of an asteroid, and his federal court case was dismissed.

The claims also collide with each other. Virgiliu Pop, a Romanian space lawyer, claimed the Sun himself to show that such claims are bogus. James Mangan registered a claim to all of outer space in Cook County, Illinois, in 1949. With no official register for such things, there is no office that could decide between them.

A notary's stamp is often taken for government approval, and it is not. A court accepting a case is often reported as a court accepting the claim. Silence from a government or the United Nations is taken as permission, as Hope has done, when it only means no one replied. A person who buys a plot receives a certificate and nothing a court is known to enforce. The International Institute of Space Law, a professional body of space lawyers, warned in 2023 that deeds to property on natural bodies in space raise the chance that individuals will be misled.

Statehood offers no way around this. The usual test, from the Montevideo Convention of 1933, asks for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the ability to deal with other countries. A star where nobody can live fails the first test before the others arise. Estimates of every kind of success here are zero.

The most workable version is a souvenir sold honestly as a souvenir. It carries no rights over the Sun or over anyone who uses its light, and it depends on the rules of whichever website and court the seller happens to use. Sunlight itself remains free to collect, since no one needs title to the Sun to put up a solar panel. Nothing can be built at the Sun, and the only activity on record is paperwork and online sales.

moon.essay:
The Moon is the natural body that circles Earth, about 385,000 kilometres away, with a radius of about 1,740 kilometres. Its gravity is one-sixth of Earth's, and its very thin atmosphere gives no protection from the Sun's radiation or from falling rocks. The ground reaches about 127 C in full sun and falls to about -173 C in darkness. Ice lies in permanently shadowed craters near the poles. It is the only other world people have walked on, so the legal questions are closest to being tested here.

The basic rules come from the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main treaty on what countries may do in space. Article I gives free access to all areas. Article II says no country may take over the Moon by claiming authority over it, by using or occupying it, or by any other means. Article IV allows peaceful purposes only, with no military bases, weapons tests or military exercises. Under Article VI, private activity needs permission and continuing oversight from a treaty country, which answers for it. Article VIII says a registered object stays the property of its owner, and the registering country keeps legal power over the object and its staff, on the surface as well. Article IX requires countries to avoid harmful contamination and pay due attention to the interests of others. Article XII opens stations to visits by representatives of other members, on a reciprocal basis and with advance notice.

The result resembles a tent on a public campsite, where the tent is yours and the ground never becomes yours. The Soviet probe Luna 2 scattered metal pennants marked "USSR" when it crashed in 1959, and they gave no claim. The descent stage and flag of Apollo 11, and the rover of Apollo 17, remain American property on ground that is not American. The same holds for China's Chang'e 4 and Chang'e 6, India's Vikram lander at the place India calls Shiv Shakti point, and Japan's silent SLIM lander. The wreck of Russia's Luna 25 is still Russian property. Firefly's Blue Ghost lander belongs to a private company, and the United States still answers for it.

A second treaty, the Moon Agreement, took effect in July 1984 after Austria became the fifth country to join. Article 11 calls the Moon the "common heritage of mankind", meaning it belongs to humanity as a whole, and says its surface cannot become the property of any country, organization or person. A future set of rules is to govern commercial use of its resources, and those rules have never been written. Article 9 lets countries build stations using only the area they need, and they must tell the UN. As of 1 January 2026 it had 17 members and 4 countries that signed without joining, and no leading space power is a member. American campaigners fought it in 1979 and 1980, and the United States stayed out. Saudi Arabia left with effect from 5 January 2024.

The newer approach is the Artemis Accords, a US-led set of principles first signed by eight countries in October 2020. They describe themselves as a political commitment, so no country can be taken to court for breaking them. NASA counts 78 signers, the latest Vietnam on 28 October 2026. Section 10 says extracting resources does not in itself count as a country taking over the body. Section 11 creates "safety zones", areas where signers give notice of their work and coordinate to avoid interference. A zone's size follows the work done there, and it ends when the work stops. NASA says this respects free access. It is the most debated part of the Accords, and no court has tested it. A US law, 51 USC 51303, lets American citizens own and sell space resources they recover, subject to the country's international obligations. China and Russia lead a rival project, the International Lunar Research Station, with construction planned from 2031. Both camps want the area around Shackleton crater at the south pole because of its ice, and Article II bars either from claiming it.

Private deeds sit apart from all this. A. Dean Lindsay of Georgia claimed space objects before a notary in the 1930s, and Robert Coles later sold Moon lots at a dollar an acre. James Mangan's Nation of Celestial Space claimed all of space in 1949 and applied to join the UN. Jenaro Gajardo Vera, a Chilean lawyer, declared himself owner of the Moon in 1954, partly to meet a social club's rule that members own property. The property registry has no record of the deed. Dennis Hope filed a claim in 1980, told the UN, treats its silence as approval, and sells deeds through his Lunar Embassy. Discover magazine reported 4.25 million buyers and over $9 million in sales. The Official Lunar Registry charges about $20 an acre. Virgiliu Pop, a Romanian space lawyer, traced these claims in his book Unreal Estate and took apart Hope's legal argument. The International Institute of Space Law, a professional body of space lawyers, warned that such deeds raise the chance that individuals will be misled. No government or court is known to back one, and a buyer receives a printed paper.

Suppose a group wants its own settlement. The first bump is permission. In the United States a launch needs a licence from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), with insurance for harm to others of up to $500 million. Radio frequencies are assigned through the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), a UN agency, and only member countries can file. The Moon Express case shows how unformed this still is. In 2016 no US agency was clearly in charge of a private landing, so the company asked the FAA, which issued a favourable review. Lawyers at the group TechFreedom doubted that one letter met Article VI, and the mission never flew. Lonestar's small data centre, marketed as beyond national data rules, reached the Moon on the Athena lander in 2025. The lander fell on its side, the mission ended in about 13 hours, and the United States answers for that hardware too.

Money comes next. A Falcon 9 rocket costs about $3,246 per kilogram to low orbit, and the Moon is much farther. Food at 2.77 kilograms a day comes to about 1,000 kilograms a person each year, or about $3.3 million at that rate. The International Space Station costs about $3 billion a year to run.

On site, no one can keep others out, because of Article I, though safety zones may limit access in practice. For All Moonkind, a nonprofit, helped pass a US law in 2020 protecting old landing sites, which binds only companies working with NASA, and Section 9 of the Accords commits signers to preserve such sites. In an emergency, Article V tells astronauts of member countries to help each other, and specialist care means going home. Crime stays under outside law, since the registering country has power over the base and US law reaches offences by or against US nationals outside any nation. American settlers would still owe US tax returns, under a 1924 Supreme Court case, Cook v. Tait.

Declaring independence would change little. The usual test of statehood, from the Montevideo Convention of 1933, requires a defined territory, which Article II closes off. UN membership requires a Security Council recommendation and two-thirds of the General Assembly.

The most workable version is a licensed base under a cooperating country, with residents' own rules made by contract and with a safety zone announced around the work. The chance of building even that is estimated at about 5 percent. Whoever arrives first with a state's support gains practical influence over a site, which lasts only as long as the work and carries no title. Residents stay subject to the licensing country.

asteroids.essay:
An asteroid is a lump of rock, metal or ice that orbits the Sun on its own. Asteroids range from boulders to small worlds, and most have very weak gravity. People are interested in them for two reasons. They might be mined for materials such as water ice, and in theory someone might one day hollow one out or build on one. No one has lived on an asteroid, and no published plan to settle one is known.

The law treats an asteroid the same way it treats the Moon. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, covers all natural bodies in space. Article II says no country may take one over by claiming authority over it, by using or occupying it, or by any other means. Under Article VI, a private group needs permission and continuing oversight from a treaty country, and that country answers for it. Under Article VIII, a craft stays under the law of the country that registered it, even after it lands. The Moon Agreement, a separate treaty that few countries have joined, applies its Moon rules to other bodies in the solar system except Earth. Those rules include a ban on private ownership of the surface. Its Article 1(3) says they do not apply to meteorites that reach Earth naturally, so a rock that falls in your field is a separate matter.

The best-known claim shows how this works in practice. Gregory Nemitz, an aerospace consultant from Nevada, claimed the asteroid Eros in March 2000 because he wanted to establish that private people can own property in space. On 12 February 2001, NASA landed its NEAR Shoemaker probe on Eros and left it there. Nemitz sent NASA an invoice for $20, the parking and storage fee for the next century. NASA refused, saying his claim had no basis in law. He wrote to the State Department, which replied that in its view Article II rules out private ownership of an asteroid. In November 2003 he asked a federal court in Reno to decide the matter. The judge ordered the case dismissed in April 2004, and the claim was dismissed on appeal in 2005. No court gave him title, and the lasting product of the case is an official American position against private ownership of an asteroid.

Paper claims continue anyway. A statement by the International Institute of Space Law, a professional body of space lawyers, says deed claims have been extended to other natural bodies in space, and one deed seller told Discover magazine that he owns about 95 planetary bodies. Fraud has appeared here too. In 1999, officials at the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the regulator of investment markets, listed share offerings for exploring a near-Earth asteroid among fraudulent internet schemes.

The real legal development concerns what is dug out of an asteroid, as opposed to the asteroid itself. A useful comparison is fishing on the open sea. No one owns the ocean, yet a boat owns the fish it catches. The United States adopted this reasoning in 2015. Title IV of the Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act, now 51 USC 51303, says an American citizen engaged in commercial recovery of an asteroid resource may own, transport, use and sell it, subject to American law and the international obligations of the US. The law also disclaims any national ownership of a body in space. Luxembourg passed a similar law on 20 July 2017, and its own Council of State, which advises on new laws, said it was unclear whether international law allows this. The United Arab Emirates followed with Federal Law No. 12 of 2019, and Japan with Act No. 83 of 2021. Section 10 of the Artemis Accords, a set of principles that countries sign as a political commitment, says extracting resources does not in itself count as a country taking over the body. Whether one country can grant rights that others must respect is still debated, and no court has tested any of these laws. None of them gives anyone ownership of the asteroid.

Suppose a company in one of those countries sets out to mine an asteroid and house workers there. It first needs a launch licence. In the United States that comes from the Federal Aviation Administration, with insurance against harm to others of up to $500 million. The craft must go on a country's register under the Registration Convention, a treaty on listing objects launched into space, and private people have no way to register themselves. That country then keeps legal power over the craft and the people aboard. Radio frequencies come through the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency whose members are countries. If the craft damages something, the Liability Convention makes the launching country pay, so that country has good reason to demand insurance and supervision.

The next problem is money. Planetary Resources announced itself in 2012, and Deep Space Industries nine months later. Both built small spacecraft and both stood to gain from the new laws. Neither mined anything. A funding round for Planetary Resources with a major mining company fell through in 2017, which led to large layoffs, and in October 2018 the blockchain firm ConsenSys bought it on undisclosed terms. Bradford Space announced on 1 January 2019 that it had bought Deep Space Industries, by then working on small-satellite engines. The writer Jeff Foust concluded that the boom had been a bubble. Japan's Hayabusa 2 brought back a few grams of dust from the asteroid Ryugu in December 2020. Transport costs make the difficulty clear. A Falcon 9 rocket delivers cargo to low Earth orbit at about $3,246 per kilogram, and that is only the first and cheapest part of a trip to an asteroid. Supplying one person with food alone, about 1,000 kilograms a year, would cost about $3.3 million at that low-orbit rate, by simple arithmetic.

People who did reach an asteroid would meet further bumps. A claimed asteroid gives no right to exclude others. Article I of the treaty keeps all of space open to every country, and Article XII opens stations on natural bodies to visits by other members' representatives. Help in an emergency could be months or years away, depending on the asteroid's path. Crime would remain under the law of the registering country and of people's home countries. Americans would still owe US tax returns, because the duty follows citizenship. A person who signs up to a self-declared asteroid nation changes none of this.

Common misunderstandings come from mixing up these layers. Owning ore is often reported as owning the asteroid. A national mining law is often taken to mean that the country has claimed territory, when these laws go out of their way to deny that. A deed from a website is taken for a title, and an invoice like Nemitz's is taken for a legal claim. The Montevideo Convention of 1933, the usual checklist for statehood, asks for a defined territory, and Article II denies that to anyone on an asteroid.

The most workable version is a licensed robotic mining company based in a country with one of these laws, which owns what it extracts and sells it under that country's law. A crewed base would follow the same pattern, with staff living aboard a registered craft under the registering country's authority. Distance would make outside control slow, which is why holding on once there is estimated at about 30 percent, while the chance of building at all is estimated at about 1 percent. Under such a law a company could own its machines and its ore, and nobody would own the asteroid.

lagrange-cislunar.essay:
The space between Earth and the Moon is sometimes called cislunar space, meaning "on this side of the Moon". It has no ground. Anything placed there is a craft that keeps moving, and the Moon itself, about 385,000 kilometres from Earth, is the far edge of the region. Within it, and in the wider neighbourhood of Earth's path around the Sun, are special positions called Lagrange points. They are named after a mathematician, and they are places where the pull of two large bodies, such as the Earth and the Sun or the Earth and the Moon, balances in a way that lets an object keep its position relative to them while using little fuel.

NASA describes five such points for any pair of large bodies. Three of the five, called L1, L2 and L3, are like a ball balanced on the top of a steep hill. Any small push moves an object away, so a craft there needs constant small adjustments to stay in place. The other two, L4 and L5, are like a ball in a bowl. If an object there is pushed a little, it tends to return. L4 and L5 sit 60 degrees ahead of and behind the smaller body along its orbit. A point is a mathematical position, and nothing about it can be fenced or occupied the way a piece of land can. For the Earth and the Sun, NASA says the nearest of these points are about five times the distance from Earth to the Moon.

The law here is the ordinary law of outer space, and no separate treaty covers this region. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, makes space free for all to use in Article I and bars any country from taking it over in Article II. Article VI makes countries responsible for space activity, including private activity, which needs their permission and continuing oversight. Article VIII gives legal power over a craft, and over the people aboard, to the country that registered it. Being at a Lagrange point changes none of that, so a craft at L5 is in the same legal position as a craft in low orbit. Two operators who both want to be near L5 have only the general duty of Article IX, which asks each country to pay due attention to the interests of others.

Two further documents add detail for some countries. The Moon Agreement, a treaty on the Moon and other bodies in the solar system, says in Article 1(2) that references to the Moon include orbits and paths around it. Its rules, including its treatment of the Moon as the common heritage of mankind, therefore reach parts of this space, but only for the 17 countries that have joined it. The Artemis Accords, a set of principles for space activity, ask signing countries to register their objects (Section 7), release scientific data (Section 8), and give notice of operations inside "safety zones" to avoid harmful interference (Section 11). The Accords describe themselves as a political commitment, so they do not create rights that a court could enforce.

The idea of living at these points has a real history. In September 1974 the physicist Gerard O'Neill published "The Colonization of Space" in the magazine Physics Today, describing colonies at Lagrange points. Keith Henson and Carolyn Meinel of Tucson, Arizona, read it and wrote to him, and in August 1975 they incorporated the L5 Society, named after the point. Its first newsletter set the long-range goal of disbanding at a mass meeting at L5. O'Neill's book The High Frontier followed in 1977. No hardware was ever built, and critics said transport costs were far too high for individuals to pay. The society's real effect was political. In 1979 and 1980 it campaigned against the Moon Agreement, arguing that treating the Moon's resources as the shared property of humanity would make space colonies impossible, and the United States never ratified that treaty. In 1987 it merged with the National Space Institute to form the National Space Society, which still operates. Later work on a design called Kalpana One reflects a change of view. The Moon's L4 and L5 points are now thought too far from the Moon and Earth, and a settlement there would spend about two-thirds of its time outside the protection of Earth's magnetic field.

Suppose a private group wants to put a small habitat at the Earth-Moon L5 point. The group needs a launching country and an entry on that country's register, in the same way as a station in low orbit. In the United States, a launch needs a licence from the Federal Aviation Administration, with insurance against harm to others of up to $500 million. The Registration Convention, the treaty on listing objects launched into space, gives private people no way to register themselves. Whichever country registers the habitat then holds legal power over it and everyone inside.

The second step is radio. The habitat must talk to Earth, and the frequencies come through the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency whose members are countries. A national authority must file on the group's behalf, and that gives that country's regulator a say over the project. Supplies are the third step. The habitat depends on Earth for radio frequencies and for deliveries, and supply runs here would be harder than to low orbit. A Falcon 9 rocket costs about $3,246 per kilogram to low orbit alone, and a person needs about 2.77 kilograms of food and 0.84 kilograms of oxygen each day. Even the International Space Station, which has reached 98 percent water recovery, relies on deliveries. It costs about $3 billion a year to run.

The fourth set of bumps concerns people. A resident needing a surgeon faces a trip of days to reach Earth. The Rescue Agreement, a treaty on helping astronauts, requires members to help spacecraft crews who land in distress and return them to the launching authority, which means a country or a qualifying international organization. A self-declared state appears to have no standing under it. Crime would fall under the law of the registering country, and US citizens would still owe US tax returns. A child born aboard would take nationality from whatever the parents' countries provide, because the Outer Space Treaty does not mention birth. One operator's debris endangers everyone nearby, and no one can fence off the surroundings.

A common misunderstanding is that a point with no ground and no neighbours must be free of law. In fact the law travels with the craft through its register. Another is that being first at a Lagrange point gives a right to stay there alone. Article I keeps it open to others, and a safety zone under the Accords lasts only as long as the work and binds only those who signed. A third is that declaring a nation at L5 could meet the usual test of statehood, the Montevideo Convention of 1933, which asks for a defined territory. A position in empty space that no one may claim does not provide one.

The most workable version is a licensed, registered station at or near one of these points, operated by a company under the supervision of a cooperating country. Residents could agree among themselves by contract how daily life is run, within that country's law. No published plan for a private settlement here is known. The chance of building one is estimated at about 3 percent, and the chance of holding on against outside control at about 20 percent, because supply lines to Earth and the registering country's authority stay in place the whole time.

geo.essay:
Geostationary orbit is a single ring around Earth, directly above the equator and 35,786 kilometres up, according to the European Space Agency. A satellite in this ring travels at about 3 kilometres per second and goes around once every 23 hours and 56 minutes, which is exactly the time Earth takes to turn. Seen from the ground, it appears to hang over one spot. Dish antennas can therefore stay pointed in one direction, and weather satellites can watch one region continuously. Three evenly spaced satellites can cover most of the planet. Only one such ring exists, which makes positions in it valuable.

Reaching it takes two stages. A craft first follows a long oval path that climbs to 35,786 kilometres, then fires its engine again at the top to round the path into a circle. Operating there then requires a filing by a country and a launch licence, and those two requirements are the heart of the matter.

The general law is the same as in low Earth orbit. Article II of the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, bars any country from taking over outer space. Article VI requires a treaty country to permit and oversee private activity, and Article VIII gives legal power over a craft to the country that registers it. The treaty does not name this orbit, and it does not define where outer space begins. That gap produced the one serious attempt to claim the ring.

On 3 December 1976, eight countries on the equator, Ecuador, Colombia, Brazil, Congo, Zaire, Uganda, Kenya and Indonesia, signed the Bogotá Declaration. They called the orbit a scarce natural resource and said the part above each signer's territory fell under that country's sovereignty, meaning its full legal control. Parts above open ocean were to be shared by all nations. Their argument was that the treaty never defined outer space, so it did not cover the orbit over their land. Many of them were newly independent and resented a rule set by countries that already had satellites. Treating the declaration as conflicting with Article II is an interpretation, since the treaty does not name the orbit, and the claim won little support. Two signers kept it in their law. Article 101 of Colombia's constitution lists its segment of the orbit as part of the country, and Colombia's Constitutional Court said in 2004 that the country had not given up sovereignty over it. Article 4 of Ecuador's 2008 constitution also asserts rights over the orbit. How a court would treat a private station parked above either country has not been tested.

In daily practice the ring is run through radio. Every satellite needs radio frequencies to work, and two transmitters on the same frequency in the same direction spoil each other. The International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the UN agency for radio and satellite coordination, keeps order. It has 194 member countries. Article 44 of its founding treaty, the ITU Constitution, says radio frequencies and orbits, including the geostationary orbit, are limited natural resources and that countries should have fair access to them. Article 45 bars harmful interference. Under the ITU's Radio Regulations, national authorities submit notices, and approved frequency assignments are entered in the Master International Frequency Register, the official global list. Filings made since 7 November 1998 carry fees to recover the ITU's costs, under Resolution 88 and Council Decision 482. People often call the result an orbital slot, which is a recorded right to use certain frequencies from a certain position. It is an entry on a list, and it is not land.

This is the obstacle that matters most. A frequency filing can only come from the national authority of a member country. A station without one would have no recorded protection from interference, and other operators would appear to have no duty to coordinate with it. A self-declared state could join the ITU only with the agreement of two-thirds of the members, if it is outside the UN.

Tongasat shows both how open and how closed this system is. Matt Nilson, a businessman who had moved to Tonga, a small kingdom in the South Pacific, persuaded its king in 1987 that even a tiny country could apply. The government authorised the venture in April 1988, and in March 1990 he applied for 16 of the 180 slots then available. Intelsat, a satellite operator, and the United States objected. The ITU agreed in March 1991 after he cut the request to six, and Tonga eventually held nine. The plan was to rent each one for $2 million a year, with half the profit going to the government. Lawyers have described this as in effect a flag of convenience for space, meaning a country that lends its registration to outside operators, and later filings came from Gibraltar, Papua New Guinea and Bermuda. Tonga could do this because it is a country. China later wanted one position and Tonga gave way in exchange for aid, and on 17 August 2018 Tonga's Lord Chief Justice ruled that the company had unlawfully received over $46 million in public money. In 2019 the court made an appeal depend on a security payment of about $15,000, and how the appeal finally ended is not known.

Suppose a private group wants a small habitat in this ring. It would need a friendly member country to file for frequencies, or to rent a position that a country already holds. It would need a launch licence, which in the United States comes from the Federal Aviation Administration with insurance against harm to others of up to $500 million. It would need an entry on a register, and the Registration Convention, the treaty on listing objects launched into space, gives private people no way to do that themselves. That country then holds legal power over the habitat and everyone aboard, so the filing, the licence and the register all lead back to a government. Costs follow. A Falcon 9 rocket costs about $3,246 per kilogram to low orbit, and this ring is far higher. The habitat would also sit in a crowded band. It would also be expected to leave at the end of its life. In 2023 the US Federal Communications Commission issued its first debris fine, to Dish Network, because its satellite EchoStar-7 ran low on fuel and stopped short of the higher "graveyard" orbit it had agreed to reach.

Everyday problems are the same as on any space station. Food at 2.77 kilograms per person per day must come from Earth, and medical care beyond first aid means a return trip. Crime falls under the registering country and under each person's home country. Americans still owe US tax returns.

Misunderstandings tend to centre on the word "slot". Holding one gives no sovereignty, no right to exclude anyone physically, and no standing as a state. The Bogotá claim is also misread as a live rule, when only two constitutions keep it and other countries have not accepted it. Standing directly over an equatorial country does not place a station under that country's law, except in the eyes of that country.

The most workable version is an ordinary licensed station, registered by a cooperating country, using frequencies that country has filed or rented. Tonga's experience suggests a small country may be willing to act as the filing partner for a fee. A private group would still need that country to apply for it, and would stay under its law and its power to withdraw. The estimated chance of building here is about 3 percent, and of holding out against outside control about 15 percent, because the station depends on its filing country for radio protection and on its licence to operate.

orbital-megastructures.essay:
A megastructure, in this context, means a human-made object in space far larger than any spacecraft flown so far. Two kinds have been proposed as places to live or work. The first is the giant space habitat, a spinning wheel or cylinder in which the spin presses people against the inner wall and imitates gravity. The second is the space elevator, a cable running from the ground up into orbit, with climbing machines carrying people and cargo along it. None has been built. They raise the same legal question as any spacecraft, and the elevator raises an extra one because it touches Earth.

The Stanford torus came from a NASA summer study at Stanford University in 1975. It is a ring 1.8 kilometres across, turning once a minute, for 10,000 residents, with a total mass of about 10 million metric tons. About 95 percent of that would be a radiation shield of raw soil from the Moon, and the site would be the Earth-Moon L5 point, a stable spot in the Moon's orbit. Kalpana One, a design revised by Al Globus in 2007, is a cylinder with a 250-metre radius and a length of 325 metres for 3,000 people. The McKendree cylinder of 1995 has a 460-kilometre radius and a length of 4,600 kilometres. The Bishop Ring of 1997 has a 1,000-kilometre radius and about 3 million square kilometres of land, close to the size of India, held in by walls about 200 kilometres high and needing carbon nanotubes, a very strong material made of carbon atoms. All remain on paper.

The cost problem is simplest to see through mass. At the Falcon 9 rocket's price of about $3,246 per kilogram to low orbit, lifting the 10 million tons of a Stanford torus from Earth would cost about $32 trillion, by simple arithmetic, before any construction. That is why the design relies on Moon soil, and using it would require an industry on the Moon that does not exist. Even the 5 percent not made of soil would come to about $1.6 trillion at that rate. For comparison, the International Space Station costs about $3 billion a year to run. Large colonies have been designed since 1975 and have never been funded, so the chance of building one is estimated at about 2 percent.

The law for the habitat is short, and it does not change with size. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 is the main treaty on what countries may do in space. Article VI says private activity needs permission and continuing oversight from a treaty member. Article VIII says the country that lists a space object on its register keeps legal power and control over the object and the people on it while it is in outer space. Article VII makes countries liable, meaning legally bound to pay, for damage caused by their space objects. Under the Liability Convention, a later treaty on that subject, a launching country pays without any need to prove fault for damage on Earth or to aircraft, and pays for damage in space if it was at fault. A launching country includes one that launches, pays for the launch, or whose territory is used. A ring with 10,000 residents would legally be the same as a small satellite with a very large crew, under one country's register. Nothing in the treaty turns an object into territory because people live on it.

A habitat built in parts by different countries could follow the International Space Station. A 1998 treaty among its partners leaves each with legal control over the modules it registers and over its own citizens on board, and no single legal authority covers the whole station.

The elevator adds a physical link to Earth. The cable is held taut by a counterweight far out in space. The stated technical obstacle is the cable material. Google X, Google's research lab, froze its project in 2014 after finding that no one had made a flawless carbon nanotube strand longer than a metre. A 2016 study by Feng Ding's team suggested small flaws could sharply cut the strength of nanotubes. Obayashi, a Japanese builder, announced in 2012 that it could build one by 2050 with an 8-day climber trip to geosynchronous orbit, where a satellite keeps pace with Earth's rotation. Nothing has been built.

Bradley Edwards worked from 2000 on a version with a thin ribbon, supported by NASA's advanced concepts institute. Construction would begin with a seed cable of 19,800 kilograms, and 207 climbers would add material until the ribbon reached about 750 tons and could lift 20 tons per climber. He proposed anchoring it on a movable sea platform in the western equatorial Pacific, to avoid lightning and hurricanes and to shift the ribbon out of the way of space debris large enough to track.

The sea anchor brings in ocean law. Ocean sites are usually in international waters, which could make talks over territory simpler. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, lists building artificial islands among the freedoms of the high seas, says no country may claim any part of the high seas, and says artificial islands get no territorial sea, the belt of coastal water that land has. So an anchor at sea creates no territory. A floating platform registered as a ship flies one country's flag, and a warship may board a ship with no nationality. A land anchor would sit under the law of the country that hosts it. Above the anchor, the cable passes through the air, then space. Over a country, the air belongs to that country under the Chicago Convention, with no stated height limit, and the boundary between air and space has never been agreed. The treaties do not mention elevators at all. Whether a cable fixed to Earth counts as a "space object" is therefore uncertain, and that affects who pays if it falls. Philip Ragan, co-author of a book on space elevators, said the first country to deploy one could control most space activities.

Fundraising has been its own hazard. LiftPort Group, founded in Washington state in 2003, announced a nanotube plant in New Jersey and a goal of launching an elevator in 2010. The plant was never built, though the company did test a 1,000-foot ribbon held up by a balloon. It faced a state penalty over an alleged illegal share offering and settled without a fine in February 2010. A 2012 Kickstarter campaign raised $110,353 from 3,468 backers, and many have reportedly asked what happened and received no reply. In April 2019 its founder admitted little progress despite more than $200,000 in seed funding.

The common misunderstanding is that size eventually creates a country. A habitat with thousands of residents could meet the population test of the Montevideo Convention of 1933, the usual checklist of statehood, yet it would still have no land the law allows anyone to hold, and it would still be on a government's register. Another misunderstanding is that an elevator in international waters escapes all states. Its platform would need a flag, and launching countries would answer for damage. Everyone aboard either structure stays within reach of the registering country and their home country, and one operator's debris endangers all the others.

The most workable version is modest, a small licensed station registered by a cooperating country, growing in stages. Voyager Station, a proposed wheel-shaped hotel in orbit covered in its own entry, shows how far such plans have got, with no funding announced as of 2024 and no construction begun. The chance of holding out against outside control is estimated at about 12 percent, because launch licensing, liability rules and, for an elevator, the anchor all stay within a state's reach.

mars-and-beyond.essay:
Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun, about half the size of Earth, with a day of 24.6 hours and a year of 687 Earth days. It is a cold, dusty desert with a very thin atmosphere, mostly carbon dioxide. Temperatures range from about 20 C down to about -153 C. It has no global magnetic field, and its atmosphere offers little protection from falling rocks. Water exists mainly as ice just under the surface in the polar regions. Only robots have ever been there. Its distance is the main thing to examine in law and in practice.

The legal starting point is the same as for the Moon. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, covers natural bodies in space generally, and nothing in it stops at the Moon's orbit. Article II bars any country from taking over a planet by claiming authority, by use or occupation, or by any other means. Article VI requires a country to authorise and keep overseeing private activity. Article VIII gives legal power over a craft and its people to the country that registered it, with no mention of any distance where this ends. Article IX imposes a duty to avoid contaminating other worlds. For the countries that have joined it, the Moon Agreement, a separate treaty with few members, extends to all bodies in the solar system other than Earth, under its Article 1(1).

There is also a scientific rulebook. COSPAR, an international committee of space scientists, keeps a Policy on Planetary Protection, an international standard on keeping other worlds free of contamination from Earth, last revised in January 2026. It works through national space agencies and has no treaty force of its own. A licensing country could still apply it to a private mission as part of meeting Article IX.

The machines already on Mars show how property works there. The Soviet probe Mars 3 made the first soft landing in December 1971 and failed 110 seconds later. It remains Russian property today. NASA's Viking 1 lander of 1976, Phoenix of 2008 and InSight of 2018 sit silent, and they still belong to the United States. So do the rovers Curiosity and Perseverance, including the sealed sample tubes Perseverance left on the ground for a later mission. China's Tianwen-1 lander and Zhurong rover remain China's after dust covered Zhurong's solar panels and it failed to wake in December 2022. In each case the country owns the machine and gains no title to the ground, because Article II bars it.

The best-known attempt to write a different rule came from a private company. In October 2020 the test-phase customer terms for Starlink, SpaceX's satellite internet service, said that for services on Mars or in transit there "the parties recognize Mars as a free planet and that no Earth-based government has authority or sovereignty over Martian activities", with disputes settled "through self-governing principles". A term in a private contract binds only the people who signed it. It cannot release SpaceX from the United States, which under Article VI must authorise and supervise it. An article in Völkerrechtsblog, an international law blog, argued that SpaceX's conduct in space counts as that of the United States, and that such a claim risks breaching Article II. A note at the University of Richmond said the clause tried to sidestep international law. The clause has never been tested, and whether the current terms still say this has not been confirmed.

Suppose a private group plans a settlement. Before departure it needs a launching country, an entry on a register and a licence. That country is responsible for the group and in legal control of what it registers. Next comes timing. Earth and Mars come nearest about every 26 months, so ships leave in batches. China's Tianwen-1 took from 23 July 2020 to 10 February 2021 to reach Mars orbit, a little over six months. Radio frequencies come through the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency whose members are countries.

Money is where the real attempts have failed. Mars One, a small Dutch venture announced in 2012 by Bas Lansdorp, planned a one-way colony paid for partly by a reality television show, at an estimated $6 billion for the first mission. It said 202,586 people applied, while Joseph Roche, a physicist among the finalists, said only 2,761 had completed the process, and the company later confirmed his figure. On 15 January 2019 the Civil Court of Basel in Switzerland declared Mars One Ventures bankrupt with debts of about 1 million euros. No hardware was built. The Mars Society, founded by the engineer Robert Zubrin in 1998, is a volunteer nonprofit whose physical work has all been on Earth, at simulated Mars bases on Devon Island in Canada and in the desert. It held contests on designing a colony of 1,000 and a city state of one million, with a $10,000 prize for the second, and it has adopted no known constitution for Mars. Elon Musk's stated hope, as reported by Universe Today, is 1,000 Starship rockets carrying 100 people per trip every 26 months, toward a million people. Such a transport system does not yet exist.

A 2020 model by the researcher Salotti in the journal Scientific Reports estimates about 110 as the minimum for a self-sustaining colony, by comparing the work required for survival with the time people have available. It holds only under the model's assumptions. No project has produced its own food at scale. Each person needs about 0.84 kilograms of oxygen a day, and space station crews used food at 2.77 kilograms per person per day, so a failed harvest would be a serious emergency when the next ship might be two years away.

Daily life brings its own bumps. No hospital would be near, and help from another world's crew under Article V of the treaty, which asks astronauts of member countries to assist each other, would exist only if another crew happened to be there. A crime would fall under the registering country and under home countries, and US law reaches offences by or against US nationals outside any nation. American settlers would still owe US tax returns every year. Children born there would take whatever nationality their parents' countries give, since the treaty does not mention birth, and whether its words about "personnel" cover a child born on Mars is not settled.

Paper claims appear here too, and they fail for the same reasons as elsewhere. In 1997 three men in Yemen complained to their Prosecutor General that NASA had invaded Mars, which they said they inherited from ancestors 3,000 years earlier. A popular history newsletter says the complaint was rejected, and no court record is known. Deed sellers also offer plots on Mars. The International Institute of Space Law, a professional body of space lawyers, has warned that such deeds can mislead buyers.

The most common misunderstanding is that distance removes the law. Distance slows enforcement, since no navy could arrive in less than months, and this is why holding on once there is estimated at about 35 percent. In law, the registering country's power continues, and a settlement relying on ships from Earth would also depend on whoever licenses those ships. Recognition as a state is estimated at about 0.2 percent, because the usual test in the Montevideo Convention of 1933 asks for a defined territory and Article II denies one.

The most workable version is a settlement licensed and registered by a supportive country, with local rules agreed among residents by contract, and growing self-reliance that gives it more practical freedom over time. The chance of building even that within 25 years is estimated at about 2 percent. Its legal status would remain that of a registered outpost.

venus-clouds.essay:
Venus is the planet next to Earth on the side nearer the Sun. Its surface is about 464 C, hotter than the melting point of lead, under an atmosphere pressing about 91 times as hard as Earth's air at sea level. Higher up, conditions change. About 50 to 55 kilometres above the ground, the temperature and air pressure come close to those on Earth. This has led engineers to propose living there in craft that float, without ever touching the ground. So a territory on Venus would mean a group of balloons or airships drifting in the clouds of another planet.

The physics explains the appeal. The atmosphere of Venus is mostly carbon dioxide, which is heavier than the mix of oxygen and nitrogen people breathe. Breathable air therefore floats there, in the same way that helium floats on Earth, with over 60 percent of the lifting power helium has on Earth. A balloon could hold the residents' own breathing air and be lifted by it. According to NASA's HAVOC study, at 55 kilometres the temperature is 27 C, the air pressure 0.5 bar (about half that at sea level on Earth) and gravity 8.73 metres per second squared, a little below Earth's. Figures from the NASA scientist Geoffrey Landis put about 50 kilometres at a pressure about the same as sea level on Earth, with temperatures of 0 to 50 C. A person going outside would need breathing air and protection from acid and some heat, and no pressure suit. A tear in the balloon would let gases mix slowly, leaving time for repairs, because the pressure is about equal on both sides. Landis argued that the atmosphere above would also shield against radiation about as well as Earth's does.

The difficulties are equally physical. The clouds contain sulfuric acid, so every outer surface must resist it. Winds at the cloud tops reach up to 95 metres per second, about 340 kilometres per hour, circling the planet about every four Earth days, and a floating city would travel with them, since tethering it would put stress on the structure. Hydrogen is very rare on Venus, which limits local water. Metals and other solid materials would have to be brought in or obtained some other way. The only human-made craft known to have floated there are the Soviet Union's Vega balloons, from 1985, and those small balloons lasted only days, until their batteries ran out.

The law is that of outer space generally. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, says in Article II that outer space, including the Moon and other natural bodies in space, cannot be taken over by any country, whether by claiming authority over it, by using or occupying it, or by any other means. Nobody therefore owns Venus or its air. Article VI says private activity needs permission and continuing oversight from a treaty country, and countries answer for what their nationals do. Article VIII says the country that lists a space object on its register keeps legal power and control over the object and the people on it while it is in outer space or on a planet, moon or other natural body. Since nothing has been built there, no one has tested whether a balloon drifting in the air of Venus counts as a space object or as use of the planet. The treaty text speaks of objects launched into space and of natural bodies. A balloon launched from Earth and carrying its passengers fits those words reasonably well. A city built there from materials gathered on site raises a harder question that has no answer yet.

Three proposals make up the record. In 1971 the Soviet engineer and science fiction writer Sergei Zhitomirsky proposed the Floating Islands of Venus, cities kept up some 50 or 60 kilometres high using technology from zeppelins and hot air balloons. He is not known to have claimed any part of Venus. In 2003 Landis presented his paper Colonization of Venus at a conference in Albuquerque. He argued that the only trouble with Venus is that the ground lies too far below the comfortable level, so settlers should live in the air. At the far extreme, aerostats, meaning craft that float like balloons, might cover the whole planet. In 2014 Dale Arney and Chris Jones, engineers at NASA's Langley Research Center, created HAVOC, the High Altitude Venus Operational Concept. It ran in five phases, from a robot airship 31 metres long to astronauts in orbit, a crew staying about 30 days in an airship 129 metres long, a one-year stay, and a permanent human presence in the atmosphere. Travel out would take 110 days and return 300, for 440 days in total. NASA later said it was an internal study for building analysis skills and never a real mission. It received no further funding and was cancelled by 2017. None of these proposals dealt with who would govern the residents.

Suppose a private group wants to build one floating station. Before anything else it needs a launching country, a licence and an entry on a register. In the United States, the licence comes from the Federal Aviation Administration, with insurance for harm to others of up to $500 million. The Registration Convention, the treaty on listing objects launched into space, gives private people no way to register themselves. That country then keeps legal power over the station and its staff, however far away they are. Radio frequencies come through the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency whose members are countries. Contamination comes next. Article IX requires countries to avoid harmful contamination of other worlds, and the licensing country may apply that to a private crew.

Money is the next bump. A Falcon 9 rocket costs about $3,246 per kilogram to low orbit, so a year's food for one person, about 1,000 kilograms, would cost about $3.3 million to lift that far, and Venus is much farther. No private funding for this is known. Each resident needs about 0.84 kilograms of oxygen a day and much more in food and water. A breakdown would be serious, because a return trip takes months and there is no ground to land on. Medical care would be whatever is aboard. The Rescue Agreement, a treaty on helping astronauts, depends on other crews and countries being able to reach the spot, and none could for months. A crime aboard would fall under the registering country's law, and citizens would stay subject to their home country's rules, including US tax returns for Americans.

A common misunderstanding is that floating avoids the ban on occupying a planet. Article II says "by any other means", so a country or its licensed company gains no claim by floating. Another is that a floating city could meet the usual test of statehood, the Montevideo Convention of 1933, which asks for a defined territory. A craft blown around the planet by winds of 340 kilometres per hour has no fixed area, and no one may claim the air it moves through.

The most workable version is a small research airship under one country's licence, with robots first, along the path HAVOC described. Distance would slow any outside control, which is why holding on once there is estimated at about 35 percent, while the chance of building at all is estimated at about 1 percent. In law it would stay a registered craft, the property of its owner, under the registering country.

outer-moons.essay:
Beyond Mars and the asteroid belt lie the giant planets Jupiter and Saturn, each with many moons, and smaller worlds called dwarf planets, such as Ceres in the asteroid belt. Some of these bodies are large and hold huge amounts of ice. Writers and engineers have suggested them as settlement sites because they could supply water, fuel and building materials on the spot. All such plans are studies on paper. No crew has been sent under any of them, and nobody has carried people this far.

Each world poses different physical problems, so a few figures help. Europa, a moon of Jupiter, has ice over a hidden ocean that may hold more than twice the water of all Earth's oceans. Its radiation is the main barrier, about 5.40 sieverts per day for an unshielded person, when about 5 sieverts over a few days is fatal. A sievert is a measure of radiation dose. Ganymede, another moon of Jupiter, receives about 0.08 sieverts per day and has gravity about 0.15 of Earth's. Callisto lies outside Jupiter's radiation belt, the zone of harmful radiation around the planet, and has gravity about 0.13 of Earth's. Titan, a moon of Saturn, has gravity 0.138 of Earth's, a thick atmosphere of nitrogen and methane, and lakes of hydrocarbons, but extreme cold and no free oxygen. Enceladus, also a moon of Saturn, has an underground ocean only tens of metres under the ice at its south pole. Gravity this low has unknown effects on bone, muscle and children's growth.

The legal position is short and the same everywhere here. Nobody owns these worlds. They are natural bodies in space, so they fall under the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main treaty on what countries may do in space. Article II says they cannot be taken over by any country, whether by claiming authority, by using or occupying them, or by any other means. Article VI says private activity needs permission and continuing oversight from a treaty country. Article VIII says the country that registers a craft keeps legal power over it and its crew, in space or on any natural body. The treaty text sets no distance limit on either rule. Since no craft has carried people this far, none of this has been tested. The Moon Agreement, a separate treaty with 17 members, also extends its ban on owning the surface to other bodies in the solar system, though only for those members.

Contamination is a further issue here. Article IX requires countries to avoid harmful contamination of other worlds. COSPAR, an international committee of space scientists, issues a policy on protecting other worlds, and its January 2026 version added a unified policy for icy worlds. Oceans under ice are places where scientists hope to look for life, so a mission to drill into Europa or Enceladus would expect close questions from its licensing country and from its national space agency. COSPAR's policy has no treaty force of its own and works through those agencies.

The published descriptions of these settlement plans do not discuss ownership or law at all. They are engineering studies. Robert Zubrin, an American aerospace engineer who founded the Mars Society, wrote in his 1999 book Entering Space that Titan was the best moon for a base. Stephen Gillett had written about Titan as a home for life in the magazine Analog in 1992. Titan's atmosphere could supply a gas for making breathing air, and water beneath the surface could yield oxygen. In 1997 the private Artemis Project drafted a plan to settle Europa, with igloos on the surface as bases for drilling, and possibly people living in air pockets inside the ice. Metals and minerals would have to be brought in, heavy shielding would be needed, and the plan was never carried out. In 2003 NASA's HOPE study, short for Revolutionary Concepts for Human Outer Planet Exploration, chose Callisto. A base there could make fuel for further exploration, and it has accessible water, silicate rock and metals. A crew's round trip was estimated at about 2 to 5 years, assuming major advances in propulsion. It stopped at the study stage.

The fourth case points to a different kind of settlement. In 2020 the Finnish space physicist Pekka Janhunen posted a preprint, a paper shared before formal publication, on a settlement in high orbit around Ceres. He chose Ceres for its nitrogen, which an Earth-like atmosphere requires. Spinning habitats joined to a disk-shaped frame would give the same gravity as Earth, mirrors would bring in sunlight, and a space elevator on Ceres would lift material cheaply. Density would stay at 500 people per square kilometre, on soil 1.5 metres deep. Each person would account for about 10 million kilograms of material. An orbiting structure of this kind would presumably be treated as a space object, though it would be built from Ceres materials and never launched from Earth. Who would register it is uncertain, because the Registration Convention, the treaty on listing objects, speaks of objects launched into space.

Suppose a private group tried. The first step would happen on Earth, as for any space mission. It would need a launching country, a licence and an entry on a register. In the United States the licence comes from the Federal Aviation Administration, with insurance against harm to others of up to $500 million, and the launching country stays liable for damage. Frequencies would need filing through the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency whose members are countries. These steps all happen before the group leaves, so the group cannot avoid them by distance.

The next bumps are the voyage and supplies. Radio messages would take many minutes each way, so no one could call for instructions in an emergency. Travel would take years, which would keep other states away and also make rescue impossible. The treaty's Article V asks astronauts of member countries to help each other, which is of little use when no one is close. A doctor, a surgeon, teachers and engineers would all need to be aboard. Nothing delivered from Earth would arrive soon, and a resident could not easily leave. Children born there would have no choice in the matter, and they would be growing up in a gravity whose effects are unknown. Their nationality would depend on their parents' home countries, since the treaty does not mention birth. Americans would still have US tax duties on paper, whatever their distance.

Common misunderstandings concern distance again. Being very far away does not end the registering country's legal power, because the treaty sets no limit. Being first on Titan does not create a claim to it, because Article II bars that and Article I keeps all areas open to everyone. A self-declared nation would still lack a defined territory, one of the four tests of statehood in the Montevideo Convention of 1933. Recognition is estimated at about 0.1 percent.

The most workable version is a research base licensed by a treaty country, on a low-radiation world such as Callisto, as NASA's study suggested, and supplied by machines sent ahead. That study assumed major advances in propulsion. The chance of building is estimated at about 0.5 percent. Once a crew had arrived, distance would give them a fairly high practical chance of being left alone, estimated at about 40 percent. The same distance would make rescue impossible, and the law would continue to treat them as under the country that registered them.

interstellar-ships.essay:
The nearest star system beyond the Sun, Alpha Centauri, is 4.34 to 4.37 light-years away. A light-year is the distance light covers in a year, so a radio message would take more than four years to get there and the same to come back. A ship that could carry people there would have to travel for a very long time. Designers therefore describe a generation ship, also called a worldship, in which people would live and die during the trip and their descendants would arrive. One report on a recent design competition describes a voyage of 250 years. No such ship exists. Crewed ships exist only as studies and paper designs.

Anyone hoping such a ship could leave every country behind first needs to understand how the law treats a ship once it has left. A ship built to travel to another star would stay under the legal control of the country that lists it on its official register of space objects. The Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, took effect on 10 October 1967, and 118 countries had joined it as of October 2025. Article VIII says the country that lists a space object on its register keeps legal power and control over the object and the people on it "while in outer space" or on a natural body in space. It gives no distance at which this ends.

Read literally, that means the ship carries its registering country's law with it for as long as the voyage lasts. A person born aboard, a century out, would appear to come under the authority of a government that person had never seen. The treaty speaks of "personnel", which is an odd word for a child born on a ship, and it does not mention birth, so whether the word covers such a child is uncertain. No court or government agency is known to have applied these articles to a voyage between stars, and no one has ruled on what happens to law on a voyage lasting many generations.

Two other articles apply before and during the trip. Article VI says private space activity needs permission and continuing oversight from a treaty country, and that the country answers internationally for that activity. Article VII says countries are liable, meaning legally bound to pay, for damage their space objects cause. These rules explain why the obstacle comes before departure. A private launch needs a country's approval. In the United States, that means a licence from the Federal Aviation Administration, with insurance against harm to others of up to $500 million and the power to block a launch on safety, national security or foreign policy grounds. The Registration Convention, the treaty on listing objects launched into space, gives private people no way to register themselves. A group wanting to leave all governments must therefore first persuade one government to approve, register and take responsibility for it. No known project has reached that stage, and the published page on Breakthrough Starshot does not discuss launch approval.

The real projects are studies. Project Hyperion was started by the researcher Andreas Hein in December 2011 from a student group at the Technical University of Munich. Its team published a study in the Journal of the British Interplanetary Society in 2012. In 2014 the researcher Cameron Smith used its data to estimate how large a population must be to stay genetically healthy over the trip. A design competition opened in 2024, with results in July 2025, and first place went to the Italian team Chrysalis. Reports do not say how such a ship would be governed.

Icarus Interstellar, a volunteer nonprofit registered in Alaska in February 2011, aims at interstellar flight before the year 2100. Its project Persephone is a design concept for a worldship 20 kilometres long and 5 kilometres across, housing 50 to 500 people. Its activity after 2015 is not known, and it has built no ship.

The 100 Year Starship began in 2010 at DARPA, the US military's research agency, which gave it $1 million, with $100,000 from NASA's Ames center. A workshop in January 2011 listed intellectual property, credibility and governance as immediate problems. In 2012 a group led by the foundation of the former astronaut Mae Jemison won a $500,000 grant and took over the name, moving the project from government to private hands. That year Senator Tom Coburn listed it among the 100 most wasteful federal spending projects. The last activity reported was a symposium in Nairobi in 2023.

Breakthrough Starshot, the one funded plan, carries no people. The investor Yuri Milner announced it in 2016. About 1,000 probes of a few grams each would ride on sails pushed by lasers on the ground, reaching 15 to 20 percent of the speed of light and arriving in 20 to 30 years. It began with US$100 million, with the final cost put at $5 billion to $10 billion. In September 2025 Scientific American reported it was on hold indefinitely, and the physicist Philip Lubin estimated that about $4.5 million had been spent. No formal cancellation has been reported. That final cost estimate is for probes of a few grams each.

Suppose a crewed ship were somehow funded and approved. The questions then follow in order. Before departure come the licence, the register, the radio frequencies coordinated through the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency whose members are countries, and the question of who insures a craft that never returns. During the trip, no rescue is possible. Article V of the treaty asks astronauts to help each other, and no one else would be near. Everything must be made and recycled aboard. Even the International Space Station, which has reached 98 percent water recovery, still relies on deliveries. The population must be large enough to stay healthy. Researchers named Marin and Beluffi estimated from simulations that a group could reasonably survive if it started with more than 98 people. Those aboard would need doctors, engineers and teachers from among themselves in every generation.

Governance is where the legal theory and practical reality separate. The ship's officers would be under the registering country's law, and a crime aboard would in theory fall under that country's courts. In practice, no police could reach them, and a message asking for instructions would take years once the ship neared another star. This is why the chance of holding on once under way is estimated as high, about 50 percent. It reflects distance alone. Children aboard would be subject to a law they never chose, though no outside authority could enforce it. The treaty's Article XVI lets a country withdraw on one year's notice, and countries can change or cease over a period of centuries. What would happen to a ship's legal status in such a case has not been addressed.

A common misunderstanding is that leaving the solar system means leaving the law. On paper it does not. Another is that a ship's company could become a nation on departure. The Montevideo Convention of 1933, the usual checklist of statehood, asks for a defined territory, and a ship in motion has none. Recognition is estimated at about 0.1 percent, as is the chance of building a crewed ship at all.

The most workable version today is the one already happening, namely research papers, design contests and small probes on paper, carried out under ordinary law on Earth. A crewed voyage would need a sponsoring country, which would keep legal control for as long as it and the treaty last.
